• handled within the last five cars of the train. 
• positioned with the boom end of the machine trailing, whether boom is attached or not. 
 
Derrick cars with booms disconnected, or heavy machinery riding on its own wheels or loaded on open top or flat cars, must 
be entrained with the heavy end in the direction of movement.

Marshalling Restrictions 
a) Trailing car tonnage : Marshall cranes, combination crane-pile drives, or other similar equipment (except crane

• Trailing car tonnage behind this equipment does not exceed 3000 tons.

b) Direction of Travel: When marked by arrows to indicate the direction of travel, Marshall the equipment to move in 
this direction. On wrecking cranes, where no direction of travel is indicated, boom may be trailing or facing the 
direction of travel. 
c) Separation:  
• Except crane CP 414232, and combination crane-pile drivers CP 414216 to 414222 inclusive, separate from  
-  the leading locomotive by at least one car, but not by more than 500 feet; or

-  Cars used for separation must have an outside length of at least 44 feet. 
d) Marshalling Exceptions: When Mechanical Services personnel supervise and accompany the movement, the 
equipment may be Marshalled: 
• anywhere in the train, provided it is separated from occupied equipment by at least one car. 
• opposite the direction of travel indicated by an arrow.

a) Before placing a crane, combination crane -pile driver, or high-rail crane in a train, get permission from the  USOC

Prone to Shifting and Subject to Damage 
Use extreme care when switching commodities subject to damage, especially when cars are partly loaded or unloaded. 
(E.g., shed, team, or industrial tracks) 
Service Equipment 
The following instructions apply when switching service equipment cars.   
a) Do not couple to or move “occupied” service equipment cars, unless authorized by the person in charge.  
b) Do not cut off in motion.  
c) Do not cut off other cars in motion towards these cars.  
d) Before coupling to or moving service equipment:  
1. Stop between 12 and 6 feet from the cars to be coupled or moved.  
(CAUTION: Ensure coupler heads are properly aligned.)  
2. Notify persons in or about the cars.  
3. Check cars to ensure all cables, hoses, temporary ladders etc., have been removed.  
4. After receiving the proper signal, couple carefully to avoid shock. 
 
Multi-Platform cars (Multi-Level Auto Racks are not considered Multi-Platform) 
        When loaded or empty: 
• Do not cut off in motion. 
• Do not allow to be struck by a car moving under its own momentum. 
TEC (Track Evaluation Car) 
• Handle with extreme care to avoid damage (Cars 63 and 64 are equipped with shock sensors.) 
• Do not pass over tracks with a hump or inert retarders. 
• Do not uncouple TEC cars and TEC locomotives without permission from TEC staff. 
• Handle as “occupied passenger equipment”, unless otherwise indicated. (This includes switching and train 
handling, when running light or deadheading, with or without the TEC staff aboard). 
• When testing, cars 63 and 64 should have the “A” end (with viewing window) trailing, unless authorized by the 
TEC staff to facilitate handling. 
Trailers or Containers 
Trailers and containers should not be cut off in motion or struck by a car moving under its own momentum. If these actions 
cannot be avoided, then ensure couplings are made at the lowest speed possible.  
Two Axle Scale Test Cars see scale test car Item 2.8 
 
2.4 Marshalling Restrictions-Equipment and Loads 
Loaded Multi-Level Autos  
Do not place loaded multi-level autos immediately behind open top cars containing coal, sand, gravel, sulphur, or similar 
commodities. 
 
Snowplows and Spreaders handled in deadhead service. 
• Marshall at the extreme rear of train. 
• Run in the direction of travel. 
• Do not marshall nose to nose.  
• See Speed Restriction Chart for restrictions while moving in train. 
• When handled in work service, employee in charge will determine placement of car in train. 
If not possible to run in the direction of travel: 
• Wings must remain properly secured. 
• Snow must not pack behind wings during movement. 
• Must be turned at first available wye or turntable. 
 
Two axle intermodal cars (Car Code QA)  
Trailing tonnage must not exceed 1,500 tons.  
 
Single Trailer on TOFC 
A single trailer on TOFC equipment with two hitches must not be loaded on the center hitch.  
 
Rear End Only 
Cars tagged, stenciled, billed as "Rear End Only" must be marshalled to the rear of the train.

Unoccupied) 
Trailing car tonnage must not exceed 2500 tons. 
Note: Train Area Marshalling messages do not indicate when trailing car tonnage exceeds this maximum.  This item also 
applies to Cabooses that have been modified for use by other departments. 
 
2.6 Bad Order 
***Bad Order*** 
A train receiving this Car Movement Restriction Message (CMRM) on any of the following documents:  
• Work Order, 
• Car Handling Report,  
• Outbound Wheel Report or 
• Tonnage Profile 
Indicates the car(s) has/have Mechanical defect(s) and subject car(s) must not be lifted or moved unless instructions are 
received from the Dispatcher that the car(s) is/are safe to travel, these instructions may or may not include Restrictions or 
Special Handling information.  In some cases, a Mechanical employee may provide the required handling instructions directly 
to the crew.  
 
In all instances, the train crew must record the handling information received, on the Crew Information form. 
 
B/O, Safe to Travel 
A train receiving this Car Movement Restriction Message (CMRM) has a Bad Order car that has been deemed safe to travel 
by Mechanical, and can/must be handled on the train, in accordance with the CMR Messages received. 
 
2.7 Loads Prone to Shifting 
Marshalling restrictions apply when lading is both in an open top car or a container in the end position on the car  and not 
protected by end bulkheads extending to top of lading. Also applies to gondolas with removable end bulkheads.  
 
Loads prone to shifting include pipe, timber, poles, metal rods, rail, or other similar material on flat cars. Other similar material 
includes coil steel not covered and/or not protected by end or special bulkheads. 
Must be Marshalled as follows: 
Separate loads prone to shifting must not be placed next to: 
• Occupied cabooses, passenger cars or service equipment cars  
• Placarded tank car (subject to the Instructions for Handling Hazardous Material).  
• Locmotive(s). 
Separate loads prone to shifting by at least two cars of any type, or by one:  
• full sized steel box car, 
• car loaded with one or more containers, or 
• bulkhead type car the ends of which extend above the load being protected against. 
 
Exception: This rule does not apply to road switchers when handling bulkhead flat cars loaded with tree length wood when 
they do not have other equipment to use as cover (subject to the Instructions for Handling Hazardous Material).  
 
Note: Unit pipe trains are restricted to a maximum of 5000 feet, excluding locomotives.  Non-unit pipe shipments on 
conventional trains greater than 5000 feet in length, are restricted to a maximum of 30 loads of pipe. 
 
Special Loads Requiring Observation 
Marshall as close as possible to the leading locomotive. 
Notification that a special load is in the train is given by:  
• train consist or protection notice.  
or  
• Operations Center. 
Note: These loads are not prone to shifting:  
• Machinery / vehicles loaded on flat cars that are equipped with special tie-down devices; 
• Bulkhead flats loaded with banded or packaged lumber that does not extend above the bulkhead by more than 
50 percent. 
• Freight car wheels loaded on special flat cars or in containers specially designed for transporting wheels. 
 
Transformers or Circuit Breakers

Break-in-two - Cars Carrying Long Strings of Rail  
• Notify Train Dispatcher immediately. Give location and all pertinent information regarding break-in-two. 
• If possible, clear the main track before attempting to re -couple. When attempting to re-couple, ensure all rails 
enter the proper compartment on the roller racks. 
• If the train is on a grade, apply sufficient hand brakes to secure cars, until air pressure behind the break-in-two 
is restored. (This prevents movement if the air brakes leak off.) Where grades are involved, it is preferable to 
handle on descending grades to set off point. 
• If the train is on level or nearly level grade, cars of rail may be safely pulled to the nearest set-off point providing: 
o The movement is made using extreme caution, and 
o Abrupt starts and stops are avoided.   
• To restore air throughout the entire train and to tie cars together at the point of break -in-two, the following 
equipment is in brackets on the side of the anchor car near the center of the rail train. 
o Two 25-ft. and one 15-ft. air hoses with connections, 
o Two 25-ft. and one 15-ft. length of 1” cable with hooks. 
 
Rail Shifting  
If one or more strings of welded rail shifts: 
• Notify the Train Dispatcher immediately. Give location and all pertinent information. 
• If possible, remove anchors and loosen tie-down bolts on displaced strings. 
• To pull strings into place, use: 
o Safety pull hoists (located in the side of the roller rack on the first car behind the tie-down car), or winch on 
“threader car” (if available). 
• After readjusting strings and recoupling cars, re-tighten all hold-down bolts and reapply anchors. 
 
Speed Restrictions - CPKC CWR trains on CN  
The following speed restrictions apply to CPKC CWR trains operating on CN Track. 
When loaded (maximum 82 cars) with 1 or more rails, do not exceed: 
• 40 MPH on straight track 
• 30 MPH on curves 
• 10 MPH through turnouts  
When empty, maximum authorized speed:  
• 50 MPH.  
Note: Loaded CPKC CWR cars (maximum 40) may be moved in regular trains on CN Track, provided the cars (including 
buffers), are Marshalled on the Head End of the train. 
 
2.13 Air Dump Cars  
Only employees who are knowledgeable in the operation of air dump cars may operate such cars in unloading  operations. 
When air dump cars are being operated, the conductor must personally supervise the handling to see  that all people are in 
the clear before charging actuating airline and before they are operated.  
• Dump cars must not be unattended while charged.  
• Dumping Reservoirs must not be charged until dumping is to begin.  
• Dumping Reservoir must be bled off after dumping is complete.  
• Employees are prohibited from riding inside air dump cars.  
• Cars must not be moved with doors open, except as necessary to clear material just dumped. 
• Empty air-dump cars will be handled on rear-end of train only.  
 Protection of Adjacent Tracks: Before charging the actuating airline or before attempting to dump air dump cars, it must be 
known that protection against movement on adjacent tracks, which could be fouled by material to be dumped, has been 
provided.   
 
Air Connections between locomotive and air dump car are made as follows:  
1. Locomotive Main Reservoir Hose to Air Dump Actuating Hose: This connection provides the air supply from the locomotive 
main reservoir to the dumping reservoirs on the air dump car. The brake pipe hoses remain coupled and angle cocks cut in 
between locomotive(s) and the air dump car(s) to allow use of train air brakes while dumping. Use extreme caution when 
uncoupling the locomotive main reservoir hose from the air dump actuating hose.  
2. Locomotive Brake Pipe to Air Dump Actuating Hose:  
This connection provides the air supply from the locomotive brake pipe to the dumping reservoirs on the air dump car. This 
method is to be used only when a connection cannot be made from the locomotive main reservoir hose and the air dump 
cars actuating hose. The following will apply when using this method:  
a. Properly secure the car(s).  
b. Separate brake pipe connection between the air dump car and the locomotive.  
c. Connect locomotive brake pipe hose to the actuating hose on the air dump car.  
d. Raise brake pipe pressure on the locomotive to 120 PSI by use of the regulating valve.  
NOTE: The air dump car actuating line is at a right angle to the pipe when cut-in and parallel with the pipe when cut-out.

2.14 Rotary Dump Coal Unloading Plants  
INSTRUCTIONS FOR OPERATING IN ROTARY DUMP COAL UNLOADING PLANTS  
Speed must not exceed:  
1. Loop Tracks ............................................................................................................................................................. 5 MPH  
2. Approaching and through dumper building .............................................................................................................. 2 MPH  
Unloading instructions:  
1. Before entering the dumper building, all locomotives must have all the windows closed and awnings down.  
2. Before spotting the first car for unloading, it must be known that all the rotary couplers are lined through the entire train. If 
the rotary couplers are not properly lined, the dumper operator must be notified of the car(s) initials, number, and the location 
in the train of such car(s) before the train is released to the power plant.  
3. Train crews must remain inside the locomotive cab. Riding on the sides of locomotives or cars while entering or moving 
through the dumper facility is prohibited.  
4. The engineer will spot cars using radio contact with the dumper operator.  
5. When the dumper operator advises that he is ready to take charge of the train, the engineer will proceed to nullify the 
alerter (if equipped).  
6. The train crew will advise the dumper that the train’s alerter is deactivated and must detrain, using caution to watch for  
close clearance, sudden movement, and footing.  
7. The train crew must not remain in the vicinity of the dumper building during the unloading. 
8. The train crew, before departing the plant, must observe the cars being unloaded in order to determine that the alerter is  
deactivated (if equipped).  
When unloading is completed:  
1. The train crew will board the locomotive(s) but will not move the train until radio or verbal contact is made with the dumper 
operator and permission is granted to proceed.  
2. The engineer will not make a reverse move without permission from the dumper room operator.  
3. If it is necessary to spot any cars to complete the unloading, the train crew will do so by pulling the train through the dumper 
building while maintaining radio contact with the dumper operator.  
4. To prevent damage to equipment, the engineer will take actions to dispose the air brake system of an overcharge.  
5. After train is released to the train crew, a Class III air brake test must be completed.

a fleet of geometry test cars that measure track geometry for compliance with the Federal Track Safety Standards.  FRA

geometry car operating instructions will be provided by the FRA prior to movement.

When a Severe Weather Warning, is received, the Train Dispatcher will: 
• Contact all trains in affected area and advise the train crews on the adverse weather condition(s). 
• Determine from crew or employees in field the local conditions they are observing.

• Train Dispatcher will notify any Engineering employees in the vicinity.

the wind warning is cancelled or weather within the area is clearing as determined by crew(s) on movement(s) and the Director

Section 3 – General Code of Operating Rules - Special Instructions  
 
All Subdivisions 
Unless otherwise specified, the following special instructions apply on the CPKC US Operations. 
 
Unless otherwise specified, special instructions apply to the corresponding rule number in the General Code of Operating Rules 
(GCOR). 
 
GLOSSARY 
Abbreviations - added to as follows: 
CS – Controlled Siding 
FIT – Field Information Terminal 
TB – Track Bulletin 
Fmr – Former 
Y– Yes 
N – No (as used in Track and Time) 
OS – Operations Supervisor 
RAS – Radio Activated Switch 
POST – PTC Operations Support Team  
 
Automated Horn System  
A system that provides an audible horn warning to traffic at public crossings at grade. The system is equipped with a visual 
indicator, such as an orange LED light in the shape of an "X", strobe light, or other indicating device visible to an approac hing 
train. The visual indicator is activated in conjunction with existing automatic warning devices and indicates the Automated Horn 
System is operating.  
 
"Begin OS" Signs  
Sign marking the beginning of OS (On Switch) circuit area for a power assisted switch. Fouling track between the "Begin OS" 
and "End OS" will cause Power Assisted Switch not to operate on electrical power.  
 
Block Register Territory (BRT)  
A method of operation in non -signaled territory where trains or men and equipment are authorized to occupy a main track or 
other than main track in limits designated by the timetable. 
 
Close Clearance  
A permanent or temporary object or structure that prevents the safe passage of an employee riding the side of the equipment.  
 
Controlled Track  
Track upon which the railroad's operating rules require that all movements of trains must be authorized by a train dispatcher  or 
a control operator.  
 
Control Point  
The location of absolute signals controlled by a control operator, or a railroad identifiable point as defined in the Timetable.  
 
Control Point Sign  
A sign used to define a control point within TWC limits.  
 
Crossing Clearance Sign (CC)  
Crossing Clearance Sign represents the clearance point where a train must stop if there is an adjacent track that crosses a road 
crossing at grade with active warning devices.  
 
Distant Signal  
A fixed signal outside a block system that governs the approach to a block signal, interlocking signal, or switch point indic ator. 
A distant signal does not indicate conditions that affect track use between the distant signal and block or interlocking signals or 
between the distant signal and switch point indicator, except where BRD (broken rail detection) limits are in effect, a Restricting 
signal may be displayed.  A distant signal is identified by a D.  
 
End of Train Device (EOT)  
Telemetry equipment that has the capability to initiate an emergency application of the train air brake system at the rear of  the 
train using the emergency switch on the head-end device.  
 
"End OS" Signs  
Sign marking the end of OS (On Switch) circuit area for a power assisted switch. Fouling track between the "Begin OS" and 
"End OS" will cause the Power Assisted Switch not to operate on electrical power.

Section 3 – General Code of Operating Rules – Special Instructions 
 
19 
 
Enroute Failure  
Following a successful initialization of the PTC system, any failure or malfunction that prohibits the PTC system from operat ing 
as intended after the train has departed an initial terminal. When required to change lead locomotive(s) at enroute crew change 
location, the PTC system will be handled as if it were the initial terminal. No train with an inoperative PTC system may depart or 
pass a designated PTC repair facility. These locations include St. Paul, Kansas City, and Shreveport.  
 
Fouling (employee or contractor) a track  
The placement of an individual in such proximity to a track that the individual could be struck by a moving train or other on-track 
equipment, or in any case is within four feet of the nearest rail.  
 
Hard Cut In (PTC)  
A state of the PTC system when PTC cut out switches are placed in the cut in position.  
 
Hard Cut Out (PTC)  
A state of the PTC system when PTC cut out switches are placed in the cut-out position.  
 
Intermodal Trains  
Trains consisting entirely of intermodal equipment and/or automotive business. 
 
Initial Terminal 
Location where the train is originally assembled.   
 
Loaded Bulk Commodity Train  
Loaded Bulk Commodity trains are defined as a train of fifty (50) or more loaded cars in a block, each weighing 125 tons gros s 
weight or more (bulk commodities), such as coal, grain, soda ash, etc.  
 
Non-controlled Track  
Track upon which trains are permitted by railroad rule or special instruction to move without receiving authorization from a train 
dispatcher or control operator.  
 
Non-enforcement State (PTC)  
A state when the PTC system is cut out, failed, degraded, disengaged, or experiencing other unenforceable conditions.  
 
Off-Track Equipment  
Machines that may be operated on the right of way foul of track.  
 
Personal electronic or electrical device   
An electronic or electrical device that was not provided to the railroad operating employee by the employing railroad for one  or 
more business purposes.  
 
Power Assisted Switch (PAS)  
A switch identified as PAS can be controlled remotely by use of a DTMF keypad located on the engine radio or the 
Conductor/Brakeman Pack set. This switch can also be controlled by a push button and hand pump located at the switch in the 
event of DTMF failure.  
 
PTC System Cut Out - a soft key cut out on Engineers PTC display or cycling the horn, penalty or emergency toggle switches 
to cut out position. 
 
Quiet Zone  
A segment of rail line, within which is situated one or a number of consecutive public highway-rail crossings at which locomotive 
horns are not routinely sounded.  Signs may be used to mark the beginning and end of a quiet zone.  
 
Rail Train  
Rail Trains consist of flat cars coupled together with or without special mountings for handling lengths of rail extending from car 
to car for transport.    
 
Railroad-supplied electronic or electrical device  
An electronic or electrical device provided to a railroad operating employee by the employing railroad for one or more business 
purposes.  
 
Soft Cut Out (PTC):  
A state of the PTC system resulting from selection of the cut-out key on the PTC display.  
 
Switch Control Signs  
Signs placed approximately 2 miles from a Power Assisted Switch. These signs mark areas where crew members must begin 
switch alignment or switch verification procedures.  
 
Tabular General Bulletin Order (TGBO) – a document providing, in a tabular format, the information or instructions contained 
in each track bulletin, which affect a train or engine within specified limits.

Track Car  
Any equipment which is designed to operate on the rail other than a locomotive or railroad car.  
 
Track is Clear  
1. The portion of the track to be used for the intended movement is unoccupied by rolling equipment, on -track maintenance-of-
way equipment, and conflicting on-track movements.  
2. Intervening public highway-rail grade crossings, private highway-rail grade crossings outside the physical confines of a railroad 
yard and yard access crossings are protected as follows:  
a. Crossing gates are in the fully lowered position and are not known to be malfunctioning.   
or  
b. A designated and qualified employee is stationed at the crossing and has the ability to communicate with trains.   
or  
c. At crossings equipped only with flashing lights or passive warning devices, when it is clearly seen that no traffic is 
approaching or stopped at the crossing and the leading end of the movement over the crossing does not exceed 15 miles 
per hour.  
3. Intervening switches and fixed derail are properly lined for the intended movement.   
4. The portion of the track to be used for the intended movement has sufficient room to contain the rolling equipment being 
shoved or pushed.  Yard access crossing means a private highway-rail grade crossing that is located within the physical confines 
of a railroad yard and is either:  
a. Open to unrestricted public access.  
or  
b. Open to persons other than railroad employees going about their normal duties, ( e.g., business guests or family 
members).  
 
Working Limits  
A segment of track within defined boundaries upon which trains, engines, and on track equipment may move only as authorized 
by the Roadway Worker (Employee in Charge) having control over that defined segment of track.

If necessary for clarity, a phonetic alphabet will be used to pronounce any letter used as an initial, except initials of rai lroads. A 
word which needs to be spelled for precision or clarity shall first be pronounced and then spelled. If necessary, the word shall be 
spelled again, using a phonetic alphabet. 
 
2.21 Electronic Devices – is changed to read as follows: 
2.21 Electronic Devices 
This rule outlines the requirements for the use of electronic devices. Crew members are jointly responsible for compliance with 
the appropriate use of electronic devices. 
 
Electronic Device - An electronic or electrical device used to conduct oral, written, or visual communication; place or receive a 
telephone call; send or read an electronic mail message or text message; look at pictures; read a book or other written material; 
play a game; navigate the Internet; navigate the physical world; play, view, or listen to a video; play, view or listen to a television 
broadcast; play or listen to music; execute a computational function; or, perform any other function that is not necessary fo r the 
health or safety of the person and that entails the risk of distracting the employee or another employee from a safety related task. 
 
The use of any electronic device is prohibited if that use would interfere with an employee’s performance of safety-related duties. 
 
Railroad Supplied Electronic Devices 
Railroad operating employees may use railroad supplied electronic devices to send or receive work related for authorized 
business purposes. Care and good judgement must always be used to ensure proper attention and concentration when 
performing any task. 
 
Railroad operating employees must not use a railroad supplied electronic device for purposes other than which it was intended 
or while: 
• Inside or outside the controlling cab of a locomotive, train or on-track equipment, unless there has been a safety briefing, 
and all crew members agree that it is safe to do so. 
• Operating the controls of a moving locomotive unless device is being used to reference a railroad rule, special instruction, 
timetable, track elevation chart or other directive and use does not interfere with any employee’s performance of safety 
related duties. 
• On the ground within 4 feet of any track. 
• On the ground and engaged in an active switching operation. 
• Riding rolling equipment during a switching operation. 
• At the controls of the locomotive and any other employee is assisting in the preparation of the train, engine(s), or on-track 
equipment, including testing of railroad equipment or brakes. 
 
Railroad authorized electronic devices may be used in the body of a business car or passenger train for railroad business whe n 
it will not interfere with an employee’s performance of safety related duties.  
 
Personal Electronic Devices  
A. Prohibited Use: 
All personal electronic devices are prohibited and must be turned off, stored out of sight and not on your person with any earpieces 
removed from the ear.

• To respond to an emergency encountered while on duty, 
• As a communication device in the event of radio malfunction. 
 
4.0 Timetables 
4.1.2 Timetable - Non-Bold Italics 
Where other figures, letters or names on a subdivision are printed in non-bold face italics, it indicates that this is shown for clarity 
purposes only and may or may not be part of the subdivision. Such as Chicago or Muskego Yard.  
 
Other locations printed in non-bold face italics, above or below a station name indicates the locations of switches or control points 
that may be used for movement authorities. 
 
Spur Track charts printed in non -bold italics are shown for information purposes and are connected to the corresponding 
subdivision so indicated in the footnotes. They are not a subdivision by themselves. 
 
4.3 Timetable Characters  
The following characters placed in the column provided in timetable indicate:  
A – Automatic interlocking  
B – General Orders  
G – Gate, normally lined against conflicting route  
I – Manual interlocking  
J –  Junction with another railroad  
M – Maintenance of Way Lock Out Mechanism for use by maintenance of way employees.  
S –  Gate, left lined in position last used or crossing protected by stop signs  
T –  Turning facility  
W– Hand throw crossover between Main tracks.  
X –  Power operated crossover between Main tracks.  
# - Where the symbol # is shown in the Station  column it will denote the location of a Control Point or Manual Interlocking.

required to stop.

men or equipment. 
 
Once the Train Reaches the Restricted Area, the speed specified by track warrant, track bulletin, general order, or radio speed 
restriction must not be exceeded until the rear of the train clears the restricted area. 
 
Yellow-red flags are used to indicate when a train may be required to stop. When Yellow -Red and Red flags are not displayed, 
that information will be included in the track bulletin, track warrant, or general order.

5.13 Blue Signal Protection of Workmen – is changed by adding new item H:  
H. When Blue Signal protection is required to perform work on a Remote-Control Locomotive, prior to establishing Blue Signal

This can be determined by ensuring:  
• There is not a Lock -Out device in the reverser slot or tag on the control stand indicating the locomotive is in remote

• The Remote/Manual change over switch is in the MANUAL position.  
 
If there is a Lock-Out device in the reverser slot or tag on the control stand or the change-over switch is in the REMOTE position,

A Remote-Control Locomotive in the MANUAL mode and without a Remote-Control Mode Lock-Out device in the reverser slot

• handbrakes are applied or released,

• employees are getting on or off moving equipment,

• when cars are left out to foul another track during switching,

ahead of a train, must advise the train that working limits have been established behind their train. Trains so informed must  not 
make a reverse movement except as prescribed per GCOR 6.4.1 (Permission for Reverse Movements) 
 
6.3 Main Track Authorization – under Joint Authority the following is added after the last bullet  
(US Eastern Region and the Kansas City Subdivision ONLY): 
Employees contacted for permission to enter joint authority limits will designate name of employee in charge and state locati on 
of their working limits. Employee in charge and employee receiving will record this information on the working limits form. O nce 
this information is received, repeated, and recorded, movements may then move into the joint limits. Once clear of the working 
limits the movement must inform the employee in charge of the working limits. 
 
If more than one employee is listed within the joint authority, one employee may be assigned as the employee in charge for al l 
other employees listed within the joint limits. The employee in charge will state this in instructions given to other movemen ts, 
giving names of other employees under their working limits. Contact with other employee(s) in this case is not necessary. 
 
Instructions and information may be relayed through the train dispatcher or other employees for the employee in charge. 
 
Trains must move at restricted speed within joint authorities. When trains are given joint authorities with other trains, contact with 
each train is not required.  
 
6.5 Shove Movements – First paragraph is changed to read as follows: 
Equipment must not be shoved until the engineer and the employee protecting the movement have completed a job briefing 
concerning how protection will be provided. Once the employee who will be protecting the shove movement is in position, verbal 
verification will be made between the Engineer and the person protecting the shove movement that will include all switches, 
derails, gates, or obstructions pertaining to shove move have either been lined properly or removed.  The employee protecting 
the shove movement must be in position to provide visual protection of the intended route of equipment being shoved, must not 
be inside of any vehicle and should not be engaged in unrelated tasks while providing protection.  
 
6.5.1 Remote Control Movements - the following is added as the second paragraph: 
When a crewmember of a remote-control assignment is required to protect the point of a shove movement and is equipped with 
an OCU, that crewmember must be in control of the movement. 
6.5.1 Remote Control Movements - under Relief of Providing Protection, Item 4 added as follows: 
4. When relieved from providing protection, the remote -control operator must remain outside of any vehicle or building until the 
movement is complete. 
 
6.7 Remote-control Zone 
A remote-control zone is a portion of tracks within definite limits designated in the timetable or special instructions. Before entering 
a remote-control zone, all employees that are not part of the remote -control crew must determine whether the zone is ac tive. 
Employees may receive active zone information from the remote-control operator in charge of the zone, an employee designated 
by timetable, or special instructions. 
 
When a remote -control zone is activated, track(s) within the zone must not be fouled with equipment, occupied, or switches 
operated until permission is granted by the remote-control operator to enter the remote-control zone.  
 
Employees occupying an active zone must comply with the instructions given by the remote -control operator. Trains operating 
through an active zone must document the time of entry and exit on the train delay report.  
 
Protection must be provided for all moves made by the remote-control operator while other employees are in the remote-control 
zone. The remote-control operator must know the track is clear and switches are properly lined after other employees are clear 
of the remote-control zone. 
 
A. Activating a Remote-control Zone 
Prior to using a remote -control zone, the remote -control operator will contact the designated employee to activate the remote -
control zone. Once activated, the designated employee will log the activation time in the remote-control logbook. Before use, the 
remote-control operator must sweep the zone to verify the track(s) are clear and all switches are properly lined.  
 
When a crossover switch is located within a Remote-Control Zone, both switches of the crossover must be restored to normal 
position after use.

B. Allowing Movements through an Active Zone 
When a remote-control operator allows a movement through an active zone, the following will apply: 
• The remote-control operator will have a job briefing with all crewmembers of their assignment and with the crewmembers 
of the movement requesting access into the active zone. The job briefing must cover switch positioning, limits authority, 
and reporting clear of the active zone. 
• Only one train or other movement may be allowed to occupy the limits of the active zone at a time. 
• If more than one train or other movement needs to enter the active zone, the zone must be deactivated. 
• When a train or other movement is clear of the active zone the remote -control operator or assigned crewmember must 
visually determine that the switches for their route are lined correctly.  
 
C. Transfer of an Active Remote-control Zone 
An active remote-control zone may be transferred between remote-control operators. A job briefing must be conducted each time 
the zone is transferred between remote-control operators and, if applicable, other authorized employee. 
 
D. Deactivating Remote-control Zone 
The remote-control zone must be deactivated at the end of a remote-control operators tour of duty, unless: 
•  The remote-control zone is transferred; or 
•  Special instructions specify the hours the remote-control zone is active. 
 
In order to deactivate a remote -control zone, the remote -control operator will contact the designated employee that grants 
activation and release the active zone. The designated employee will document the time it was deactivated in the Remote-control 
Zone Log. 
 
E. Zone Log Records 
The designated employee that grants the activation of the remote -control zone at a minimum must document the following 
information on the required form: 
Date: _________________________ Designated Employee: ___________________________ 
 
Zone ID Engine Number Employee In Charge Time Activated Time Deactivated Transfer Time 
      
 
6.9 Meeting or Passing Precautions - is changed by adding a sentence, which will now be the last sentence of the 
second paragraph:  
A train that will be met or passed at a Power Assisted Switch must not line the switch for the opposing or passing train.  
 
6.14 Restricted Limits - Rule does not apply on CPKC. 
 
6.20.1 Key Trains or Equipment Left Unattended with Hazardous Material  
A Key Train or equipment that defines a Key Train may be left on a main track or siding with train dispatcher permission.  
When so left the crew member will communicate with the train dispatcher and provide the following information: 
• Number of hand brakes applied.  
• Train Tonnage.  
• Train Length.  
• Location and track staged on indicating: 
o Grade of track, such as, tangent, ascending or descending. 
o Terrain of track, such as, straight or curving.     
• Weather Conditions. 
• Type of Equipment Secured such as mixed freight or unit train. 
Train dispatcher will confirm with train crew that the train or equipment is secured in accordance with securement rules. 
Exception: 
When an on-duty crew is performing the following activities listed below, equipment may be left unattended without locomotive 
attached when equipment is secured in accordance with securement rules.   In addition, the equipment must not be left 
unattended or off air for more than 24 hours.  
• picking up, setting off, or repositioning cars at an industry. 
• assembling cars from several tracks adjacent to the main track. 
• adding, removing, or swapping locomotives; and 
• moving part of the train when doubling a hill or cutting crossings. 
 
Alert Material cars must be attended in High Threat Urban Areas where they are staged in line with US Hazardous Material 
Instructions for Rail Section IX Item 39 (c).

6.21.1 Protection Against Defects – the following is added to the first paragraph as last sentence: 
A train must immediately reduce to 10 MPH and perform a pull by inspection or passing train inspection on at least one side of 
the train. 
 
The following is added after the first paragraph: 
If a train operating at restricted speed discovers a broken rail, before completing movement over it, train must stop and wait for 
maintenance personnel to determine if it is safe to proceed or if repairs must be made. Permission for train to proceed must be 
received from the train dispatcher or control operator. 
 
1. When a movement has been advised by the train dispatcher that an Unidentified Track Occupancy (UTO) inspection is

form, noting “UTO inspection". 
3. In situations where the crew has been advised by the Train Dispatcher to inspect and it is further determined that the UTO 
was not caused by railway equipment, the Train Dispatcher will advise the crew that they are relieved from performing the 
inspections required for an UTO.  The crew must draw a line through any related entry on the Crew Information/Train Brake 
Status form and enter "UTO cancelled" with the date, time, and Train Dispatcher initials for the UTO that was removed. 
 
6.21.3 Track Obstruction/Unusual Condition - Rule does not apply on CPKC. 
 
6.23 Emergency Stop or Severe Slack Action - Inspection of Cars and Units is added to as follows: 
Inspection must be made of all cars, units, equipment, and track. It must be known by inspection that equipment and track are  
in safe condition that all wheels are properly positioned on the rail and train is complete before proceeding.  
 
After inspections are completed, the train dispatcher must be notified of the inspection results before proceeding. 
 
A. Emergency Brake Application 
Trains that are stopped by an emergency brake application must make a pull -by inspection not to exceed 10 MPH after the 
brakes are released as indicated by the end of train device or air flow indicator, on at least one side of the train to check  for 
evidence of defective or derailed equipment. At locations where a pull-by inspection cannot be made, the train may proceed not 
exceeding 10 MPH to the first location where a pull-by inspection can be made.  
 
B. Severe or Unusual Slack Action 
If severe or unusual slack action was experienced when stopping or if excessive power is required to start train, a walking 
inspection of the train must be performed before train can be moved. When walking conditions make it impracticable, inspect as 
much of the train as possible, then train may be moved not to exceed 5 MPH until inspection can be completed. If excessive 
power is required to move the train, train must be stopped immediately, and the cause determined for the use of excessive 
power.

C. Pull-by Inspection Not Required 
A pull-by inspection will not be required if all of the following conditions are met: 
• Emergency brake application is not the first occurrence for that train consist.  
• Train tonnage is less than 6000 tons or train tonnage is 6,000 or more and each car exceeds 100 gross tons. 
• Speed at time of emergency brake application was greater than 25 MPH.  
• The emergency brake application occurs within 15 seconds of initiating a service brake application. 
• No severe or unusual slack action is experienced during the stop. 
• When brakes are released, the air flow indicator and the rear car brake pipe pressure readings indicate no loss of air 
pressure. 
• Train contains no loaded placarded tank cars, or a car, trailer or freight container placarded “Explosives A.”   
 
If train does not meet all the above requirements a visual inspection must be made as outlined under Item A or B. 
 
D. Derailment Inspection 
If a derailment has occurred and crew is instructed to handle a portion of their train beyond the derailment, the crew must inspect 
all cars before movement can be made, paying attention to journal boxes, shifted loads, side bearing clearances, etc. If cars are 
left at site of derailment, it must be ascertained that the cars have been inspected and if not, train crew must inspect befo re 
moving cars. 
 
Engineers must inspect all units in the consist. 
  
6.29.1 Inspecting Passing Trains – following is added to the first paragraph: 
Unless relieved of the responsibility, any on-duty crew is required to perform passing train inspections at crew change 
locations. 
 
Crew that is in CDS service and/or will encounter hours of service issues, must contact the train dispatcher, and be governed 
by instructions received.    
 
This means: 
• The outbound crew is expected to be in position to meet the inbound crew. 
• When the outbound crew is on duty, inbound crews must remain on-duty and position themselves to perform outbound 
inspection. 
 
If the outbound crew is not yet on duty, inspection must alternatively be performed by any available qualified employees at a 
crew change location, as the train is either inbound or outbound. 
 
6.29.1, Inspecting Passing Trains, under Ground Inspections, is changed to read as follows: 
For Employees Under an Hourly Agreement or Trip Rates on the former SOO, DM&E, D&H, CMQ and KCS Properties:  
 
When a train is stopped and is met or passed by another train and when duties and terrain permit, all crew members must inspect 
the passing train from the ground on both sides of the track.  
 
If terrain does not permit, inspection for opposite side, all crew members will be on the ground next to their train to provided 
inspection.  
 
The engineer of the standing train must: 
• If possible, stop the train at a location that allows an employee to perform the inspection from the opposite side of the 
track. 
• Perform the inspection from the ground on the same side as the standing train so that it is not left unattended. 
 
If being passed by another train, the train to arrive second must notify the first train when they pass the approach to the s iding, 
to allow all crew members to be in position for inspection. 
 
EXCEPTION: Crew members in Deadhead service while deadheading by train are exempted from the above requirements. Crew 
members of passenger trains are exempted from the above requirements except when at meeting points in single track territory. 
However, every effort must be made to stop a movement when a dangerous condition is noted. 
 
For Employees under a Non-Hourly Agreement on the Southern Region Properties:  
When a train is stopped and is met or passed by another train and when duties and terrain permit, the Trainman must cross the 
track and inspect the side of the passing train opposite the stopped train. If terrain does not permit, inspection for opposite side, 
the Trainman will be on the ground next to their train to provided inspection. 
 
The Engineer of the standing train must: 
• If possible, stop the train at a location that allows an employee to perform the inspection from the opposite side of the 
track. 
• Perform the inspection from the locomotive cab of the standing train so that it is not left unattended.

When a train stops en route, a walking and/or roll by inspection of as much of the train as is possible must be made as time 
and conditions permit.  This does not apply to passenger trains. 
 
6.30 Receiving or Discharging Passengers – is changed to read as follows: 
When a passenger train is receiving or discharging passengers the following will apply: 
a. Train, engine, or on-track equipment must not pass between the standing train and the station platform being used.  
 
A scheduled passenger train or an extra passenger train that will make a station stop that will result in receiving or 
discharging passengers across a main track or controlled siding intervening between the train and the stations platform 
must make a radio announcement “(Train) approaching (station) will be making passenger stop on (track)”  
 
The train will also be required to make a radio announcement to advise other movements when it begins leaving the 
station stop. 
 
Extra passenger trains approaching a station stop will make a radio announcement “(Train) approaching (station) will 
be making a passenger stop” and will make an additional announcement before leaving the station “(Train) departing 
(station)”. 
b. Train, engine, or on -track equipment approaching on an adjacent track must not pass that train, unless one of the 
following safeguards are established: 
 
• Intertrack fencing is provided and affected pedestrian crossings are blocked,  
or 
• A crew member is stationed at the rear of stopped passenger train to prevent pedestrians from crossing and 
pedestrian crossings are blocked.  
c. A passenger train must not depart a station when a train or engine is seen approaching until the leading end of 
approaching train has passed rear of standing train unless communication has been established to ensure safeguards.  
d. At initial stations, when trains that are standing near crosswalks, a crew member must be in position to protect passengers 
against approaching movements on adjacent tracks.  
 
Train or engine on an adjacent track must ring bell approaching and passing a passenger train at a station and sounding engine 
whistle, as necessary. 
 
6.32.1 Providing Warning Over Road Crossings – is changed to read as follows: 
When cars are shoved, kicked or a gravity switch move is made over road crossings at grade, an employee must be on the 
ground at the crossing to provide warning until crossing is occupied.   
 
Make any movement over the crossing only on the employee’s signal.  
 
Warning is not required when crossing is equipped with:  
• Gates that are in the fully lowered position.  
or  
• Flashing lights or passive warning devices (cross-bucks, stop signs, etc.) when it is clearly seen that no traffic 
is stopped at the crossing or is approaching the crossing. Leading end of shoving movements must not exceed 
15 MPH over crossings.  
 
Within a yard, this only applies to crossings open to unrestricted public access. 
 
6.32.2 Crossing Warning Devices (Highway/Pathway-Rail Grade Crossings) will remain in effect as written in the GCOR 
8th Edition with the following exceptions: 
1. Procedure 3 does not apply on territories covered in the US Eastern Region Timetable and the Kansas City 
Subdivision.  
2. C&M (Rondout to Customer Union Station), Egin, and Fox Lake Subdivisions are governed by separate instructions 
outlined below.

or

C. Power Off Indicators 
When the power off indicators on the side of signal housings at crossings are flashing or not illuminated, immediately notify the 
train dispatcher. 
 
6.32.7 Automatic Warning Device Power Indicator lights –rule applies only on former DME property.  
Crossing signal cabins are equipped with a white power indicator light which burns steadily while commercial power is available 
to the signals. The light will be extinguished or will emit a white flashing strobe light when commercial power is out. Emplo yees 
must notify the train dispatcher when the power indicator light is extinguished or flashing and must report the location of the 
crossing.   
 
7.0 Switching 
7.3 Additional Switching Precautions – first bullet changed to read: 
• Passenger or outfit cars – Must be switched separately and not handled with other types of cars during switching 
operations.  
New bullet added after the second paragraph:  
• Cars loaded with railroad wheels  
 
7.6 Securing Cars or Engines – the following is added as the last paragraph:  
The locations of Hump or Bowl yards will be designated in the Timetable Subdivision/Branch Special Instructions.  
 
7.7 Kicking or Dropping Cars  
Kicking or dropping cars is permitted only when it will not endanger employees, equipment, or contents of cars.  
 
Dropping cars is permitted only at locations where specifically indicated by special instructions.  
 
Before dropping cars, crew members must fully understand the intended movement. They must verify that the track is sufficiently 
clear, and that switches and hand brakes are in working order. If possible, the engine must run on straight track. Cars must not 
be dropped over spring switches or dual control switches.  
 
7.7.1 Gravity Switch Moves the following 3 bullets are added under When making a gravity switch move: 
• None of the cars are placarded. 
• The hand brake used to control the move is a vertical wheel style on a car with proper hand holds, ladders or platform 
to maintain 3-point contact. 
• The switch is lined for the intended route prior to making the switch. 
 
7.11 Charging Necessary Air Brakes - is changed to read:  
Do not handle cuts of cars without charging the air brake system unless the cars can be handled safely and stopped within the

8.0 Switches 
8.2 Position of Switches – added as last paragraph: 
Crew members must confirm the position of the switch in accordance with GCOR 6.1.1(Verbal Communication) and before  
leaving the location of a main track switch, the employee handling the switch will transmit the following over the radio channel:  
 
“(movement identification) (occupation) (name)(Switch location) LINED, LOCKED AND CHECKED in (normal/reverse) position.”

35 
 
8.3 Main Track Switches – the following is added to the sixth bullet for TWC territory: 
Switch must not be considered restored to normal position until confirmation is received back from the employee reporting. 
Employees reporting a normal position switch must be at the switch or moving over the switch on the main track when report is 
made. 
 
8.8 Switches Equipped with Locks, Hooks, or Latches - is added to as follows: 
A switch equipped with a switch point lock pedal will be identified by a white or yellow stripe on both sides of the switch stand or 
switch handles painted white or yellow. The pedal must be depressed before operating the switch.  Crews need to ensure that  
locks are secured on both the switch and switch point lock after use. 
 
8.12 Crossover Switches - is added to as follows: 
When switch tenders are on duty for handling main track switches for crossover movements, the following procedure must be 
followed: 
1. Switch tenders on duty must have a copy of the track bulletin or a message in the exact words of the track bulletin prior 
to commencing the day’s work. 
2. Main track crossover switches must not be lined for crossover movement until advised by the train dispatcher. 
3. Crossover switches must be lined far enough in advance to afford block signal protection. 
 
8.16 Damaged or Defective Switches - is added to as follows: 
When switches are spiked, they will be identified by a tag or tape attached to the switch stand or handle. This does not relieve 
the requirements of additional protection as required. 
 
8.18 Variable Switches - rule does not apply on CPKC property.  
Crews are to hand line all trailing movements through switches regardless of if it is a variable switch or not. Designated sp ring 
switches are the only switches that would be able to be trailed through when not lined for the movement. 
 
8.19.1 Radio Controlled Switches (RCS) or Power Assisted Switches (PAS) 
The location of Radio-Controlled Switches or Power Assisted Switches and operating instructions will be designated in the 
timetable and/or special instructions.  
 
A Radio-Controlled Switch or Power Assisted Switch can be remotely controlled by using the radio keypad on the channel so 
indicated under the subdivision footnotes, or by using a push button located at the switch in a box mounted on the signal case.  
 
At Radio Controlled Switch or Power Assisted Switch locations there will be "Begin OS" and "End OS" signs marking the limits 
of the on switch. In order for the RCS or PAS to operate by DTMF or by push button located at the switch; the limits of the OS 
must not be occupied.   
 
8.19.2 Operating a Radio-Controlled Switch (RCS) or Power Assisted Switch (PAS)  
To operate a Radio-Controlled Switch (RCS) or Power Assisted Switch (PAS), a crew member must perform the following:   
Upon passing the wayside sign reading "switch control" (Placed approximately 2 miles from an RCS or PAS), a crew member 
must enter the proper DTMF sequence for the desired switch position.   
 
NOTE: Switch Control signs installed less than two miles from an RCS or PAS location will be noted in the Timetable.   
 
To enter the proper DTMF sequence:   
To line the switch to the normal or reverse position, enter the code found in the Timetable. After entering the proper DTMF 
sequence, you must receive radio confirmation that the switch is properly lined for requested movement.   
 
A train must approach an RSC or PAS prepared to stop short of the OS until:   
1. A DTMF command has been issued to request the switch for the desired position and radio confirmation message has 
been received that the switch is properly lined for desired movement. Crew on movement must repeat radio messages 
received from a radio-controlled switch.  
or   
2. The switch point indicator displays the switch is properly lined, as per GCOR 8.10, for the requested movement.   
 
The switch point indicator will convey the following indication to the movement:  
Green – radio activated switch is lined and locked for main track movement.  
Flashing Red or Yellow – radio activated switch is lined and locked for diverging movement.  
Red – Stop, inspect switch, and then operate dual control switch by hand in accordance with GCOR 9.13.1.  Permission to 
hand operate is not necessary if movement authority is granted beyond switch or movement is to take siding.  
Dark – Stop, inspect switch, and then operate dual control switch by hand in accordance with GCOR 9.13.1.  Permission to 
hand operate is not necessary if movement authority is granted beyond switch or movement is to take siding.  
 
If a movement receives a dark or red indicator it must be reported to the train dispatcher/operation supervisor.  
 
Dark indicator will indicate one or combinations of the following conditions.   
• That the RCS or PAS is unable to verify request  
• The RCS or PAS switch is not locked in position

36 
 
NOTE: If the train has not passed the Switch Point Indicator within 10 minutes after a confirmation message is received that the 
switch is properly lined for movement, the train must approach the RCS or PAS prepared to stop. 
 
8.19.3 Radio Controlled Switch (RCS) or Power Assisted Switch (PAS) Failures 
A train must approach an RCS or PAS prepared to stop if:    
1. Message "Switch Not Lined" is received.   
or   
2. NO MESSAGE is received following a request and the switch point indicator indicates the switch is not properly lined.   
 
The train must:   
• Stop short of the OS.   
• Notify the train dispatcher.   
• A crew member must operate the switch by hand as outlined in rule 8.19.4 (Hand Operation of Power Assisted Switches)   
 
If radio confirmation is received that the switch is properly lined, and the switch point indicator displays a RED or DARK, the crew 
must:   
• Stop the train before entering the OS, if consistent with good train handling.   
• Inspect the switch.   
and   
• Report it to the train dispatcher. 
 
8.19.4 Hand Operation of a Power Assisted Switch (PAS)  
Power Assisted Switches operated by hand are considered hand -operated switches, and all rules  governing hand-operated 
switches apply, except cars must not be dropped over the switch.  
  
A. Equipped with an Electric/Hydraulic Switch Machine   
To operate an electric/hydraulic RCS or PAS by hand:   
• Unlock the pump handle and the hand throw cover.   
• Select the direction of desired switch point travel by moving the directional lever.   
• Insert the pump handle and move the handle back and forth.   
• Line the switch for the intended route.   
• Examine the switch points to see that they fit properly.   
• Return the pump handle to the holder and secure it with a switch lock.   
B. Radio Controlled Switch or Power Assisted Switch equipped with a Dual Control Switch Machine To operate a RCS 
or PAS that has a dual control switch machine by hand:   
• Unlock the switch lock.   
• Place the selector lever in the HAND position.   
• Operate the hand throw lever until the switch points are seen to move when the lever is operated, even if the switch is 
lined for the intended route.   
• Line the switch for the intended route.   
• After at least one unit or car has passed over the switch points, the employee must return the switch to power by 
restoring the selector lever to the POWER or MOTOR position and lock, unless otherwise instructed by the control 
operator.      
 
When the selector lever is in the HAND position the switch point indicator will display RED, and  movements will be made as 
directed by a crew member at the switch.     
 
Position of switch does not have to be reported to the train dispatcher unless the switch is left in hand operation.  
 
All maintenance of way movements must hand operate the Radio-Controlled Switches as outlined per GCOR 9.13.1, permission 
from control operator is not necessary to hand operate these switches.   
 
8.19.5 Change of Original Requested Route  
If a change is needed from the original requested route, the train crew must stop the train outside the limits of the OS at t he 
Radio-Controlled Switch or Power Assisted Switch and:   
1. Wait 15 minutes and then enter the proper DTMF sequence to line the switch for the desired route.   
or   
2. Wait 15 minutes and operate the push button located on the signal case to line the switch for the desired position.   
or   
3. Operate the hand pump mechanism to the desired position. Examine the switch to ensure points fit properly and then 
proceed. 
 
8.20 Derails Location and Position, the following is added as the last sentence: 
Portable Derails used for protection at night or under other conditions of limited visibility must be equipped with a functioning red 
light or a Red reflectorized flag.

A train may comply with the next signal’s indication when its aspect can be clearly seen, and the signal governs the track where

governing signal will allow the train to proceed, or increase speed, the train may proceed com plying with the signal indication

or increase speed, the train may proceed complying with the signal indication governing the next block.  Passenger trains 
operating in push/pull service must not exceed 40 MPH until the next signal is visible and that signal displays a proceed indication. 
 
9.9.1 Approach to Automatic Interlocking  
A train must proceed prepared to stop at the interlocking signal when:  
• Moving below 25 MPH and passing a signal that governs the approach to an automatic  interlocking.  
or  
• Speed is reduced below 25 MPH after passing a signal that governs the approach to an automatic interlocking.  
 
When the Automatic Interlocking contains an Interlocking Approach (IA) circuit, IA milepost locations will be listed in the Timetable 
Subdivision Special Instructions and may be identified in the field by "Begin Interlocking Approach" signs. The train must proceed 
prepared to stop at the interlocking signal when: 
 
• Speed is at or reduced below 25 MPH after passing a milepost location designated as the beginning of the Interlocking 
Approach (IA) circuit.  
 
The train must continue to move prepared to stop at the interlocking signal until the train reaches a point approximately 1,000 
feet from that signal. If the interlocking signal, then indicates proceed, the train may resume speed.  
 
9.12.1 (CTC Territory) and 9.12.2 (Manual Interlocking) the following is added as last sentence to third bullet:

instructions. If required to operate release box, train must pull to within 200’ of signal before operating. After complying with the 
instructions that allow the train to proceed, if signal continues to display a Stop indication, the train must move at restricted speed 
after receiving a signal from the employee on the ground at the crossing. However, if there is a conflictin g movement, the train 
must not proceed until the movement has passed or stopped, and both crews agree on the next movement. 
 
At an automatic interlocking where push buttons are provided on signals to enable a return movement to be made over the 
crossing while switching, crew member will unlock box and press button. If signal does not clear, requirements of GCOR 9.12.3 
must be complied with.

Rule 15.1 – Track Bulletins – under Receipt and Comparison of Track Bulletins is changed to read as follows: 
RECEIPT AND COMPARISON  
At their initial station, unless otherwise instructed by the train dispatcher or special instructions, the conductor and engineer must 
each receive and have a copy of the Tabular General Bulletin Order (TGBO) affecting their train’s movement on a main trac k. 
Any pilot or snowplow foreman must each be in possession of the TGBO for their movement. 
 
The conductor and engineer must confirm and initial the train designation, the TGBO designated limits, and each page of the 
TGBO and then sign the last page of their TGBO.  Other crew member(s) will be required to read and understand the TGBO 
then initial and sign the TGBO they reviewed. 
 
All crew members must ensure that their movement is properly designated on the TGBO, it contains the correct number of pages 
and that the designated limits cover the specified routing.   
 
If it will not cause delay to movement, freight trains and road switchers should contact train dispatcher to confirm and veri fy 
TGBO number. 
 
A train specific TGBO will be addressed to a train symbol, assignment number or schedule number, and must be compared to a 
train consist, list or other acceptable document for verification.  If an incorrectly designated TGBO is received train dispa tcher 
must be contacted for further instructions or changes before proceeding. Engine identifying number is not required on a TGBO. 
If a movement receives a TGBO that shows NIL for Track Bulletins, contact the Train Dispatcher to verify the information before 
acting on the TGBO.    
 
At locations where yard limits are in effect and a train or engine cannot get their train specific TGBO, they may use a gener ic 
default TGBO to perform work within yard limits.  Crew must obtain their train specific TGBO before going outside of yard limits.   
Passenger trains that do not have a schedule number will be addressed using engine number adding direction as applicable.  
 
When a crew member receives a TGBO from the Field Informational Terminal (FIT), once verified that the document is correct, 
the crew member will acknowledge the prompt on the screen of the FIT before leaving. If the TGBO is pulled from the FIT by 
anyone other than a crew member, such as a Clerk, they will acknowledge the prompt on the screen by entering their Occupation, 
Initials and Last Name and check the box as the Acknowledger. The crew is still responsible to verify that the information 
contained in th e document is correct. If unable to obtain a TGBO from the FIT or FAX contact the train dispatcher for further 
instructions.  
 
TGBO’s will have lines in ascending order. Lines must be checked for ascending sequence, if they are not, then that TGBO is 
not complete, crew member must communicate with the train dispatcher and be governed by instructions received. 
 
All crew members are responsible for complying with the requirements of track bulletins in the TGBO and for reminding each 
other of those requirements.

15.2 Protection by Track Bulletin Form B –add Item C Work Groups:  
C. Work Groups Working Under Form B Track Protection 
1) Single Work Groups:  While working with a single work group within the limits of a Form B and all members of the work group 
are within view, the EIC of the Form B may allow a train to enter a Form B up to a specific identifiable location that is not occupied 
by the single work group.  Alternatively, if all on-track equipment and employees of the single work group are not within view, the 
EIC of the Form B may allow a train to enter a Form B up to a specific identifiable location after visually or verbally ascer taining 
that all on-track equipment and employees of the single work group have travelled past (in the direction of the train movement 
to be authorized) the identifiable location to be used as the limit for the train authority (see schematic below).   The single work 
group may continue working as long as the work location is outside of the track segment that the train has been given authori ty 
to proceed to within the Form B and sub working limits for both the work group and train are recorded on the sub working  limits 
form. 
 
 
2) Multiple Work Groups:  When multiple work groups are present and working within Form B Limits, the EIC of the Form B will 
follow the procedure for a single work group and require each additional work group to fill out the working limits form with their 
Name/Other ID and each work group will also fill out sub working limits in order for the EIC to record and track the number a nd 
location of work groups within the Form B Limits.   When required to clear trains through a specific segment of track, the 
Name/Other ID recorded in the sub working limit segment to be authorized for train operation must report clear and record as 
clear on the working limits form.

placing an out of service tag on the lock or with the placement of a secure derail and red flag at the beginning of the out of service

15.12 Relief of Engineer or Conductor during Trip – under Comparison of Information is changed to read: 
Comparison of Information 
The relieving conductor and engineer must compare mandatory directives, TGBO, instructions and pertinent information with 
each other and the train dispatcher before proceeding. 
 
When a TGBO compare is required, the crew must provide the identification number of the subdivision TGBO to the train 
dispatcher who will repeat such to the crew. If correct, the crew member must acknowledge as correct.   
 
The train dispatcher must transmit applicable track bulletin and track bulletin cancellations, if any to relief crew. 
 
15.13 Voiding Track Bulletins is changed to read: 
15.13 Canceling Tabular General Bulletin Order and Voiding Track Bulletins 
TGBO and track bulletins in the possession of train or engine crew are in effect for the entire tour of duty unless canceled, expired 
on time or a new TGBO is received. 
 
A crew in the possession of a train specific TGBO will report to the train dispatcher when train or engine has reached its fi nal 
terminal, cleared the TGBO limits, ties up at the end of a shift (including interim release) or when the use of the TGBO is n o 
longer required, unless relieved by 15.10 Retaining Track Bulletins or advised otherwise by train dispatcher. The report 
information may be relayed to the train dispatcher by the yardmaster or by telephone answering service, where available, by 
giving the train symbol, date, time, occupation, and name of employee. 
 
The train dispatcher must not release a TGBO from the computer system until they have ascertained that the train has cleared 
the TGBO limits, crew has tied up (including interim release), train is clear of the main track, or the crew is removed from the 
train. The information from yardmaster or telephone answering system may be used to release a TGBO from the system. 
 
When required, a TGBO may be canceled verbally by the train dispatcher but not until both the conductor and engineer have 
been advised. The employee who acknowledges the cancellation to the train dispatcher must advise all crew members 
accordingly. 
 
The train dispatcher may verbally cancel a track bulletin by stating: 
• Track bulletin No (number) is canceled (dispatcher’s initials). 
 
Train crew receiving will fill in the appropriate cancellation portion and repeat the information back to the train dispatche r. If 
correct, the train dispatcher will respond OK stating time and train dispatcher initials. 
  or 
The train dispatcher may verbally cancel a TGBO stating: 
• TGBO No (number) is canceled at (time) (dispatcher’s initials). 
 
Train crew receiving will fill in the appropriate cancellation portion and repeat the information back to the train dispatche r, 
acknowledging the cancellation by stating occupation and name.

17.0 RULES APPLICABLE ONLY IN AUTOMATIC TRAIN CONTROL (ATC) TERRITORY  - entire chapter does not apply 
on CPKC. 
 
18.0 Rules Applicable only in PTC Territory – title and rule is changed to read:   
18.0 Rules Applicable only in Positive Train Control (PTC) Territory 
PTC is an overlay system designed to assist crews in the safe operation of their train and does not relieve employees from 
complying with any rules or regulations.   
 
18.1 Positive Train Control - second paragraph added as follows: 
PTC Operation is not required for MOW equipment such as hi -rail, specialized maintenance, or other similar equipment, which 
may consist of one or more units operated from a single control stand – actively working in engineering service. 
 
18.3 Broken or Missing Seals – is changed to read:   
Unless authorized, do not break the protective seals on PTC devices. 
 
18.4 PTC Cut Out – is changed to read:   
The PTC system may only be cut out or disabled when authorized.   
 
1. Unauthorized disabling of a PTC system or circumventing a PTC enforcement by manually cutting out the pilot valve/brake 
stand when not authorized is a revocable event for the locomotive engineer and/or conductor responsible and subjects any other 
crewmember responsible to individual liability proceedings, including disqualification and/or civil penalties.   
2. Mechanical Requested Cut Out: Mechanical can request the crew to cut out PTC to support troubleshooting activities. The 
cut-out activity does not authorize the moving of a controlling locomotive by train crews.    
 
18.6 Consist Data – Second paragraph added as follows:  
When inputting train length, the actual train length will be used. Train Length including the 3% is not to be used.
