sections.text:
Section 3 – General Code of Operating Rules – Special Instructions 
 
43 
 
18.8 PTC System Inputs and Prompts is added to as follows:  
When authority is required, confirmation of authority must be obtained prior to pressing the received or acknowledgement key.    
 
18.9 Use of Restricted Mode is added to as follows:  
Restricted mode must be used for the following activities.    
Restricted mode must be exited immediately when completed with activities.     
• Setouts  
• Switching enroute  
• When required to clear in order to meet on account of train length  
• To reduce walking distance to a crossing at grade in order to provide warning as required by PTC onboard for a 
bulletined crossing    
• When loading/unloading of work trains under direction of MW Employee in Charge Track out of service  
 
Prior to coming out of Restricted Mode, the reverser must be in the direction of travel.   
 
When entering the Main Track for head room PTC must be active. It is prohibited to travel between stations leaving PTC in 
restricted mode.    
 
18.13 Working with Manned Helpers – add new rule:   
When a manned helper is added to the head end of a train in PTC territory and becomes the controlling locomotive, the PTC 
system on the helper must be initialized.    
 
When a manned helper is added to the rear end of a train in PTC territory, the PTC system on the helper must be cut out. No 
changes are required to the PTC system on the controlling locomotive when a manned helper is added to the rear of a train. 
 
18.14 Movements with Inoperative PTC System – Changed to read as follows:  
Immediately notify the train dispatcher when the controlling locomotive’s PTC system fails to initialize or becomes inoperati ve 
enroute, except when operating where PTC is suspended by Mandatory Directive.  
 
When a PTC device on the controlling locomotive becomes defective, the train must not pass the next designated PTC repair 
facility.  
 
If the PTC System on the controlling locomotive becomes inoperative while enroute or you are unable to initialize PTC, unless  
otherwise restricted, the following speeds will govern:     
 
In non-signaled territory, or when operating against the current of traffic in Rule 9.14 (Movement with the Current of Traffic) 
territory:     
­ Trains transporting one or more loaded cars containing TIH/PIH ……..........30 MPH     
­ All other trains ……………………………………………………………………..40 MPH     
­ In signaled territory:     
­ Freight trains transporting one or more loaded cars containing TIH/PIH ....... 40 MPH     
­ Freight trains not transporting loaded cars containing TIH/PIH ……….……. 49 MPH     
­ Passenger trains ........................................................................................... 59 MPH              
 
Where the PTC system is a method used for delivering authorities and restrictions, the train must not exceed Restricted Speed  
until advised by the train dispatcher that an absolute block has been established in advance of the train.   
 
18.15 Movement without PTC (Southern Region only excluding the Kansas City Subdivision) - add new rule:   
A train may operate in PTC territory without the controlling locomotive being PTC equipped or initialized, provided the movement 
is engaged in freight switching, transfer train service (including yard, local, and industrial), hostling, work train service , or the 
assembling or disassembling of trains, under all of the following conditions:  
a) The movement originates in a yard, or within 20 miles of a yard with the yard as the final destination point.  
b) The movement does not travel in excess of 20 miles from the point of entry onto PTC-equipped main track.  
c) The movement must not exceed Restricted Speed unless all the following requirements are met:  
1. No other train or locomotive is operating in the same authorized limits without operational PTC.   
2. No roadway worker has working limits on any part of the same authorized limits.   
3. A Class 1, 2 or Transfer Train brake test has been performed in which case the movement must not exceed 30 MPH.   
 
18.16 Training/Qualification - add new rule:  
Only PTC qualified employees are authorized to operate PTC enabled equipment within PTC territory.

sections.title: Section 3 – General Code of Operating Rules – Special Instructions
sections.text:
Section 3 – General Code of Operating Rules – Special Instructions 
 
44 
 
18.17 Departure Test - add new rule:  
A PTC departure brake test must be performed:  
• During Initialization if:  
o A successful departure test has not been completed within the last 96 hours.  
o The Onboard PTC system has been rebooted since the last departure test.  
o The PTC circuit breakers have been placed in the “ON” position since the last departure test.  
o The CUT-OUT switches have been moved to the “CUT IN” position since the last departure test; or  
o The previous departure test was unsuccessful.  
• When the “DEPART” flag is displayed on the CDU.  
or  
• When instructed to do so by the Mechanical Department or the PTC Help Desk.  
 
The brake pipe pressure must be above 75 psi to perform a departure test.  
 
18.18 Loss of Electronic Display Functionality - add new rule:   
Should the Engineers PTC electronic display (CDU) become inoperable:   
Immediately stop the train consistent with good train handling and contact the train dispatcher and be governed by their 
instructions.  
 
Trains must not continue movement until:   
• The electronic display returns to normal operation.   
or   
• The train is authorized to proceed without operative PTC in accordance with 18.14 Movements with Inoperative 
PTC System.  
 
18.19 Light Engine Moves - add new rule:   
When operating light locomotives or a train with less than 5 cars on PTC enabled track with 100% of the air brakes properly 
functioning on each locomotive, the independent brake valve handle must not be actuated if the PTC system initiates an 
application of the brakes.  
 
18.20 Reporting to the Train Dispatcher - add new rule:   
The engineer must report the following conditions and occurrences to the train dispatcher:   
• Any discrepancies between the PTC display and any mandatory directives, rules, wayside system, or other onboard 
system.  
• Any time PTC indicates train braking is in progress.  
• The train is stopped due to a PTC warning.  
or   
• PTC is suspected of not providing a warning when it should have.   
 
When making a report to the train dispatcher or the PTC Help Desk, you must include the locomotive initials and number along 
with the following information:   
a.  unable to initialize the PTC system.       
b.  experience a sync failure.        
c.  there is a PTC induced braking event.        
d.  discrepancies are found between information on a PTC display versus signal aspects in the field.      
e.  PTC is suspected of not providing a warning when it should have; or        
f.   encounter other problems with the PTC system.       
g. If problems occur when cutting in the PTC system, the help desk must be notified immediately. 
i. Time and location of occurrence. 
h. Any unusual occurrence/conditions which may have contributed to the problem.  
 
18.21 Reverse Movements in PTC Territory - add new rule:   
When making a reverse movement where PTC is in effect, the restricted speed requirement is enforced by PTC. Trains making 
a reverse movement must comply with GCOR 6.4. When moving the reverser from forward to reverse (or reverse to forward), 
wait 15 seconds in order for  the locomotive engineer to verify that the PTC Onboard display has properly updated the orientation 
of the train with respect to the map displayed (i.e., the mileposts and terrain in advance of the train has been reversed fro m its’ 
previous orientation) before moving the train.

18.22 Restricted Speed in PTC Territory - add new rule:  
PTC will enforce a 20 MPH maximum speed when entering authorized limits requiring restricted speed. The PTC system will 
provide an over speed warning at 18 MPH and over speed braking enforcement at 21 MPH. The actual speed which allows a 
train to stop with in 1/2 the range of vision will not be enforced by PTC. The crew is still responsible for adhering to the 
requirements of GCOR 6.27.

operating at restricted speed inside a joint authority.  
 
18.23 Electronically Received Permission and Authority to Occupy Main Track from the Train Dispatcher or EIC - add 
new rule:  
When required to receive verbal permission, or authority, to occupy the main track from the train dispatcher or an EIC, DO NOT 
press the “RECEIVED” or “ACKNOWLEDGE” soft key on the PTC CDU until permission, or authority, has been received and 
“OK’d” by the train dispatcher or EIC. Train crews must not enter or operate within track limits requiring verbal permission, or 
authority, to occupy without first receiving the verbal permission, or authority.  
 
This also applies to work zones, enter main track and passing a signal indicating stop.

Section 4 – Radios 
 
Transmitting Technique 
The efficient use of a radio depends on the speech and articulation of the sender.  Speak all words plainly in a clear, distinct 
tone to prevent the running together of consecutive words.  DO NOT SHOUT.  Avoid any tendency to accent syllables artificially 
or talk too rapidly.  Speak slowly and clearly. 
 
The following points should be kept in mind when using a radio: 
Position of Microphone:   Microphone should be angled at approximately 45 degrees, not more than 2 to 3 inches from the 
mouth of the sender. 
Speed:  Keep the rate constant, neither too fast nor too slow.  Remember in many cases the person receiving your message 
has to write it down. 
Pitch:  Remember, that high pitched voices transmit better than low pitched ones. 
Rhythm:  Preserve the rhythm of ordinary conversation.  To separate words so that they do not run together, avoid the 
introduction of sound that does not belong such as “er” and “um.”   Attempt to maintain the pitch and rhythm of voice to the end 
of each sentence.

outlined in the Radio Channel table 
a. Use the UT channel (if available) to call the Engineering Services Reliability desk, Diesel Specialist or PTC Help Desk. 
Note for locomotive operators: to reach the ATM/Yardmaster, tune your radio to either the road channel or local yard channel 
and dial call-in code 7.

Section 5 – Trackside Warning Detectors 
 
1.0 Trackside Warning Detector  
1.1 General 
Trackside Warning Detectors operate for trains in either direction on the track in which they are installed. Each detector type and 
location are listed in each subdivision footnotes along with recall codes, where provided, and will indicate one or more of the following: 
 
Detector Type Description  
Hot Box (HBD) Detects overheated journals. Hot Box alarms can also be caused by overheated 
traction motor suspension bearings and sticking brakes. 
Dragging Equipment (DED) Detects equipment dragging between or near the rails. 
High Wide Load Detector (HWLD) Detects shipments exceeding acceptable height and width dimensions.  
High Water Detector Measures water level near track and indicates using a signaling system of 
condition requiring train crew stop. 
Wheel Impact Load Detector (WILD) Measures excessive wheel impact on rail and identify defective cars using AEI 
car tag IDs. 
Additional information from Detector Description  
Axle Count Counts axles in train and reports it after entire train passes the detector. May 
include axle location as part of a defect message. 
Temperature 
Measures outside temperature and reports it after the entire train passes the 
Trackside Warning Detector. Temperature may be used in the application of Hot 
and Cold Weather Temperature Speed Restrictions. 
 
1.2 Alarm Announcements and Procedures while Approaching/Passing Trackside Warning Detectors 
As the train passes the detector, the talker transmits an alert tone and announcement for each alarm. The following table summarizes 
the announcements and procedures when approaching and passing a Trackside Warning Detector. 
 
Alarm Announcements while passing a Trackside Warning Detectors 
Alarm Type Announcement   
Hot Box  Tone + “hot box” or Tone + “hot journal” 
Dragging Equipment  Tone + “dragging equipment” 
Hot Wheel Tone + “hot wheel”  
High Wide Load Tone + “high load” or Tone + “wide load” or Tone + “high car” 
High Water  No tone 
When approaching a Trackside Warning Detector 
Locomotive Engineer  Must avoid prolonged use of train brakes where practicable, until the entire train passes the 
detector.  
All Crew Members Must ensure the train radio is on the correct standby channel.  
When the train reaches a Trackside Warning Detector 
Locomotive Engineer  
DMD (Distance Measuring Device) - Set the DMD as soon as the train reaches the detector 
location. Distance helps identify defect location and identify when to expect the final results 
message. Axle count is unavailable until the rear of the train passes over the detector. 
All Crew Members 
 
Radio - Avoid using the radio system until after the final results message has been transmitted. 
(This prevents talking over a tone or announcement.) 
Verbal Communication - Confirm, while passing the detector, any defects announced. 
The final announcement message lists defects starting with nearest to the head-end. Location is given by axle number from the front 
of the train, including locomotive axles. 
 
Note: Trains equipped with a steam locomotive(s) are exempt from trackside warning detector readouts unless supervising officer or 
train crew deems inspection to be necessary. 
 
Note: When notified that a trackside warning detector is temporarily removed from service for maintenance, trackside warning 
instructions do not apply and train may proceed, except Key Trains which are governed by 1.11 No Defect Found - Key Train, Alert 
Train, or Key/Alert Train.

Note (False Alarm):  Train crews may be informed by the Dispatcher that an inspection is not required due to a false alarm as 
determined by the Communication Center. If it is determined to be a false alarm, the Conductor will verbally acknowledge this report 
from the Dispatcher and the train continues. If the train has already stopped and the conductor is in the process of inspecting but 
has not reached the affected car and the Dispatcher informs them of a false alarm, the inspection must be stopped and the conductor 
must return to the locomotive, unless the Conductor has already reached the affected car, the inspection will be performed.

When an incomplete radio message, no radio message, or trackside warning detector not working message is received or train 
moving too slow, train will immediately reduce speed to 30 MPH and continue at that speed until an inspection is made by anot her 
detector or both sides of train are inspected by other employees.  If the detector is in advance of a critical structure or if two 
consecutive systems fail, a roll-by ground inspection of both sides of the train must be made at that location at a speed not exceeding 
10 MPH. Trackside inspections account of a detector failure may be performed by another train crew, mechanical employee, 
maintenance of way employee, or other qualified employee as long as both sides of the train are inspected at a speed not exceeding 
10 MPH. If possible, the inspection must be performed before the head end of the train reaches the critical structure. The train must 
be inspected when the rear of the train is no more than 2 miles from the detector.  
 
Note: The letter (C) following the detector type in the TRACKSIDE WARNING DETECTOR table indicates a detector that is in 
advance of a critical structure. The letter (N), (S), (E) or (W) designates the direction a train must be traveling to encounter a critical 
structure after exiting the designated detector.   
 
1.4 Dragging Equipment  
 
 
1.5 Hot Box 
 
When an alert tone is followed by the announcement “hot box” …  
Step Action  
1 Note the DMD reading. 
2 
Immediately reduce to Slow Speed using throttle modulation and dynamic brake, and without using the air brakes, if 
possible.  
• If a subsequent announcement states “dragging equipment” or the train will pass over a facing point switch, 
then stop immediately and follow the procedure for dragging equipment. 
3 
Observe the train for defects. If the defect is visible from the cab of the locomotive or there is an  
obvious indication of a derailment, then stop the train immediately and inspect. (See item 1.9 Procedures for Locating 
Defects) 
4 
When the rear of the train has passed the HBD, and the final results messages have been reported.  
• allow a crew member to detrain, and  
• pull the train ahead, not exceeding 10 MPH, to the defect.  
Note: If an inspection point is designated, then proceed, not exceeding 10 MPH (without stopping) to the inspection 
point.   
Note 
If the final results message reports more than six alarms, stop the train immediately and perform a stationary inspection 
(dragging equipment procedure applies).  
Exception: an uninspected portion of the train will not pass over a facing point switch, a pull -by inspection or 
combination standing/pull-by inspection is permitted at a speed not exceeding 5 MPH.  During the  
pull-by portion, the back of the hand inspection should be used to test for overheated bearing(s).  A stationary inspection 
must also be performed for any suspect defects found and at the location where the “hot box” announcement(s) was 
broadcast, based on DMD calculations.  
Note If the final results message reports “No Alarms” then resume speed and proceed without an inspection. 
5 
Perform a stationary inspection at the defect location.  
a) Locate the defect using the axle count as per item 1.9 Procedures for Locating Defects.  
b) See item 2.1 Hot Box Inspection–Friction and Roller Bearing, to test for overheated bearings. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
When an alert tone is followed by the announcement “dragging equipment” … 
Step Action  
1 Note the DMD reading. 
2 Stop the train immediately using good train handling practices. 
3 
Perform a stationary train inspection.  
a) If the entire train passes the HBD location before stopping, then locate the defect using the  
axle count as per item 1.9  Procedures for Locating Defects). 
b) If the train is stopped before the entire movement passes the HBD, then locate the defect using the noted 
DMD distance as per item 1.9  Procedures for Locating Defects). 
Note 
Do not pull ahead to a crew member to perform the inspection unless it is unsafe to walk back. If it is unsafe to walk 
back, then pull ahead not exceeding 5 MPH to inspect for defect.  
If the train must be pulled ahead over a facing point switch, do not exceed 5 MPH.

1.6 Hot Wheel 
  
When an alert tone is followed by the announcement “hot wheel” …  
Step Action  
1 Note the DMD reading. 
2 
Immediately reduce to Slow Speed using throttle modulation and dynamic brake, and without using the air brakes, if 
possible.  
• If a subsequent announcement states, “dragging equipment” or “hot box”, then follow the procedure for that 
alarm. 
3 Observe the train for defects. If the defect is visible from the cab of the locomotive, then stop the train immediately and

When the rear of the train has passed the HBD, and the final results messages have been reported.  
• allow a crew member to detrain, and  
• pull the train ahead, not exceeding 10 MPH, to the hot wheel defect.  
Exception: If an inspection point is designated, then proceed to the inspection point, not  
exceeding Slow Speed and perform the inspection. 
Note: If the final results message reports more than six alarms, stop the train immediately and  
perform a stationary inspection.   
Exception: Provided there are no alert tones followed by a “hot box” or “dragging equipment” announcement, a pull -

Perform an inspection.  
a) Locate the defect using the axle count as per item 1.9 Procedures for Locating Defects.

When an alert is followed by the announcement “high load”, “wide load” or “high car” … 
Step Action  
1 Note the DMD reading. 
2 
Immediately reduce to Slow Speed using throttle modulation and dynamic brake, and without using the air brakes, if

When the rear of the train has passed the detector, and the final results messages have been reported.

1.8 High Water Detector 
• For trains travelling in centralized traffic control (CTC) territory high water detectors are integrated into the signaling system. 
The high -water detector may trigger a track occupied light. Train crew is required to act accordingly using good train

Section 5 – Trackside Warning Detectors 
 
51 
 
 
1.9 Procedures for Locating Defects 
 
Step Action  
1 
• Note the axle location of the defects stated in the final results message, or  
• Determine the approximate location of the defect by using the noted DMD distance and train consist 
information  
2 
If determining defect location by axle count, locate the defects by counting the actual axles from the front of the train, 
beginning with the lead locomotive. Ensure cars and locomotives with other than four axles are not counted as having 
four axles. 
3 
• If defect is other than dragging equipment, a pull -by inspection to the point of the identified defect, may be 
made provided if there is no obvious indication of derailment and speed of inspection does not exceed 10 
MPH. 
• If a defect indication is for dragging equipment, a walking inspection must be made while the train is stationary. 
While performing the walking inspection and conditions no longer permit safe walking, the train may be pulled 
ahead not exceeding 5 MPH to the identified axle. 
4 
Inspect the train in the specified location.  
• If a defect is found at or near the indicated location, then inspect both sides of the train for 8 axles in each 
direction from the suspected defect. (This helps verify that the defect has been correctly identified.)  
• If a defect is not found at the indicated location, then inspect both sides of the train for 16 axles in each 
direction from the indicated location. 
• If a defect is detected at a High or Wide Load Detector, in addition to checking the location specified, two cars 
(or two platforms) ahead and behind the reported location must also be inspected, even if defect is found at 
the reported location. 
5 If any part of the train passed the HBD at 8 MPH or less, then inspect the entire train for additional defects. 
6 Notify the Dispatcher of the inspection results and take appropriate action  
(e.g., make repairs, set off car, etc.). 
7 Complete the required reporting documentation.  
8 If the defect was a suspected hot box and no defect was found, see item 1.10, No Defect Found. 
Note - Alarms from hot wheel detectors and dragging equipment detectors can only indicate the general vicinity of the alarm, 
rather than an exact location. During inspection process, be governed by Section 2 Train Inspection Procedures 
 
1.10 No Defect Found  
If no defects are found after the inspection process, train may proceed at maximum authorized speed, watching train according ly, 
except Key Trains will be governed by 1.11 No Defect Found – Key/Alert Train. 
 
When a Hot Journal/Hot Wheel alarm is received and no defect is found the inbound crew must notify the connecting crew of any  
defects providing the defective equipment initial and number, axle count(s), side of car(s) and defect(s). If the last system encountered 
failed, the inbound crew must notify the connecting crew of such failure. If connecting crew is not available this information must b e 
properly documented and left on the console of the lead locomotive. When a Hot Journal alarm is received on an axle that has been 
previously marked with a “W” the car must be set out.  
 
Second Defect within 75 miles 
Whenever a car or engine is identified by an alarm for the defect “hot box” at the same axle location twice within 75 miles car or engine 
must be set out of train. 
 
Exception:  Business car CP 99 (Display car) is equipped with a low -slung generator that when operating may trigger a false “Hot 
Box” alarm. Providing business car personnel perform a bearing temperature test and no excessive temperature is present, CP 99 is 
exempt from the requirement of setting it out of train.  
 
Second Defect in Succession 
When the same car or engine is identified by an alarm for a defect at a second trackside warning detector in succession, the car or 
engine must be set out of the train regardless of whether or not a defect can be found. While moving car to be set out, you must 
maintain a speed that will ensure safe handling of the car, but not exceeding ten (10) MPH.   
Notation must be made on the Crew Information Form and train list of car(s) showing the location of detector(s) that indicate d car 
defect. 
Note: The above does not apply to Amtrak trains. See Amtrak Equipment – Second Alarm procedure. 
 
Amtrak Equipment – Second Alarm 
When the same axle actuates a second wayside trackside warning detector, and no defect is found which may have caused the 
actuation, after the prescribed inspection, the following actions will be taken:

Section 5 – Trackside Warning Detectors 
 
52 
 
 
Step Action  
1 The train will not exceed 30 MPH for the next five (5) miles. 
2 The train will be stopped at that point and all bearings on car which activated the detector(s) will be reexamined. 
Equipment ahead of and behind the suspected axle(s) need not be reexamined during this 5-mile inspection. 
3 If any apparent increase in bearing temperature is noted during the 5 -mile re-inspection, the car will be set out at the 
first available point. 
4 
If no hot bearing is found during the 5 Mile inspection, the train dispatcher will be notified, and the train may proceed at 
normal speed to the next point where railroad mechanical personnel are available to inspect the car and authorize 
further movement or direct the car to be set out. If any station stops are made before the mechanical inspection 
point, the crew will inspect the car at such locations. 
5 
When a train actuates a trackside warning detector before a crew change location, the relieving crew will be advised of 
the equipment that activates the detector so that they can inspect the car and follow the above procedure if the 
equipment actuates a subsequent detector en-route. 
 
1.11 No Defect Found – Key Train, Alert Train, or Key/Alert Train 
If no defects are found, a Key Train, Alert Train or Key/Alert Train will not exceed 30 MPH until it has passed over the next  working 
trackside-warning detector or is delivered to a terminal for a mechanical inspection. If the same car sets off the next trackside-warning 
detector or is found to be defective, it must be set out from the train.  
 
When a Key Train, Alert Train or Key/Alert Train is informed that a trackside-warning detector is out of service the Key/Alert Train will 
be restricted to 30 MPH from the out of service trackside-warning detector to the next working track side warning detector. 
 
1.12 Trackside Warning Detector - Alarm Reporting Exceeded 
When a trackside warning detector exceeds 6 defects, the trackside warning detector will report too many alarms and then repo rt a 
malfunction. 
 
When this type of alarm is sounded, train must be promptly stopped, and a stationary train inspection must be made at the rep orted 
axle locations and the rest of the entire train on both sides to the rear of the last reported axle location must be inspected. 
 
Notation must be made on Crew Information Form and train list of cars showing the location of detector(s) that indicated car defect. 
 
1.13 Incorrect Axle Count 
When a trackside warning detector indicates a one axle plus or minus difference in comparison with the number of axles known to be 
in the train, proceed at maximum authorized speed. 
 
When a trackside warning detector indicates a 2 -axle difference in comparison with the number of axles known to be in train, be 
governed as follows: 
 
Step Action  
1 Advise train dispatcher of incorrect axle count and arrange to verify the trains consist information. Train may continue 
to move at maximum authorized speed. Key Trains will proceed not exceeding 30 MPH to next detector. 
2 If the train is carrying an additional car or cars and any of these are hazardous, arrange for a radio waybill. Update 
the position-in-train document for hazardous materials. 
3 
Continue to the next trackside warning detector and verify axle count with that detector.  If the axle count still does not 
match, stop, and perform a pull by inspection.  During inspection, pay close attention to wheel condition and low-
hanging equipment next to wheels, i.e., cables, banding, chains, or plastic wrapping. 
4 If no defects are found after inspection, the train may proceed at maximum authorized speed.  Notify the train 
dispatcher of the results and continue watching train accordingly. 
5 Communicate the correct information to the next outbound crew or proper supervisor. 
 
Note: The above does not apply to Amtrak trains. 
 
1.14 Wheel Impact Load Detector (WILD) 
Wheel Impact Load Detectors (WILD) measure excessive wheel impact on the rail. These locations are indicated under individual  
subdivision columns marked by (WILD). 
 
The train dispatcher will inform the train crew of the maximum authorized speed that the train may travel with defective equi pment 
and if required, set out instructions for equipment involved. If car is to be moved beyond a crew change point, the train dispatcher will 
inform the relief crew or yardmaster of the defective equipment and other instructions as necessary. The conductor will show this 
information also on the Crew Information Form in the section marked “Other information to subsequent crews” for relief crews en route 
while car is being handled.

2.0 Train Inspection Procedures 
When informed by a trackside warning detector or other source of a possible hot wheel, hot bearing or dragging equipment, an 
inspection must be made.  This alarm may result from abnormal heat from wheels (sticking brakes), journals, traction motors, or 
suspension bearings. At trackside warning detector locations, also comply with trackside warning detector instructions. 
 
2.1 Hot Box Inspection–Friction and Roller Bearing 
 
A 
 Required Equipment:  
All crew members, other than locomotive engineers, of each movement must be in  possession of a temperature 
indicating  crayon (150ºF). 
B 
 Crayon Application:  
 Use crayon as per illustrations in Diagrams 1, 3 and 4 below.  
 Crayon may not melt at or below freezing. 
C

• Inspection for suspected overheating must include the use of the temperature indicating crayon or if no crayon is

When inspecting for an overheated or hot wheel, pre-departure or while en route the wheels should be checked for heat discoloration

A possible cause of an overheated or hot wheel is sticking brakes. 
 
a) Detection/Description:

• Usually caused by sticking brakes or set hand brakes.  
b) Safety Defect:

Section 5 – Trackside Warning Detectors 
 
54 
 
 
Actions to be taken: 
1 
Check for sticking air brakes and determine why the brakes are sticking. Possible causes for sticking brakes include: 
• Overcharged air brake system. 
• Hand brakes applied. 
• Retaining valve not in EXHAUST position. 
• Leak in the air brake system. 
• Placing the automatic brake handle in release while the brake pipe reduction is still  
exhausting. 
• An insufficient brake pipe reduction to ensure proper release. 
• Binding or fouled brake rigging. 
• Excessive brake pipe leakage. 
• Defective control valve. 
2 
 If the brakes are successfully released, then perform a pull-by inspection of the car to ensure: 
• Wheels are turning freely, and 
• All skid and shell marks are detected 
3 If the brakes cannot be released, If necessary, cut out the car control valve and set the car out at the first available 
location or location designated in the Timetable. 
4  Complete Crew Information Form and report to the Dispatcher. 
 
2.3 Dragging Equipment 
In case of dragging equipment indication, STOP the train immediately using good train handling procedures and perform a walking 
inspection to the indicated location. Look for equipment or material that extends below the ball of the rail. Common items to look for 
are hanging brake shoes, brake shoe keys, brake riggings, low hanging air hoses, tie-down bands, wire, or chains. When defect is 
found and repaired or it is safe to move the equipment, a roll -by inspection of the remainder of the train must be made with speed 
not exceeding 10 MPH.   
 
Clear dragging equipment if possible for safe running, and if not safe to run, the car should be set out at the nearest point. 
 
2.4 Other Wheel Defect Inspections 
When inspecting wheels for a wheel defect, look for broken flange, thin flange, broken rim, loose wheel, flat spots, wheels with metal 
build up, extra-long brake shoe keys, brake rigging hanging down or dragging.  
 
To determine if a wheel is loose, examine it for the following: 
1. Excessive spacing between the wheel flange and the rail. 
2. Heavy cuttings on the wheel flange. 
3. Particles of metal on the inside of the wheel seat or axle. 
4. A shiny area on the axle near the wheel. 
5. Oil seepage around the wheel seat and axle. 
 
If no defect is found, perform an audible inspection by listening for sounds of a broken wheel, flat spots, or any other defe ct that 
may be present. Audible inspection will be performed by positioning yourself 10 cars ahead of the reported defect and roll the train 
by 20 cars listening for indications of a defect. If no axle number is given, an audible inspection of the entire train must be completed. 
 
Set the car out if a sound is heard suggesting a broken wheel (thumping sound) or any other sound or visual indication that m ay 
indicate a defect. 
 
2.5 Warm Wheel Notification Process 
The Warm Wheel Notification Process is like the WILD Detector procedure, in that the hot box detectors will be used to monitor for 
sticking brakes or hand brakes based on increased wheel temperature levels.  These levels are lower than those that would normally 
trigger a hot wheel alarm. 
 
If a sticking airbrake/handbrake is identified, an alert message will be generated to the Dispatcher that will advise of the alarm type 
and what recommended actions to be communicated to the train crew. This is separate from a sticking brake alarm that is broadcast 
from the detector itself. 
 
Crews are also reminded of the requirement to ensure that an effective 10 psi reduction is made to ensure that it propagates 
throughout the train before the release is made.  
 
The following indicates the process when a warm wheel notification is received from the Dispatcher.

2.0 Protection Notices  
A protection notice affords protection only upon Main Tracks, Sidings, Interchange Tracks, or other tracks specifically identified in 
the protection notice.  
 
2.1 Format of Protection Notices  
Format of the protection notice has been divided into 6 sections: 
 
“Section 1”:   Lists e-mail addresses which receive a copy.  Specifies the file number, the classification, and indicates if the 
shipment is governed by Specific Restrictions.  
• A file number commencing with “DL” indicates that General Restrictions apply (e.g., DL4011109).  
• A file number commencing with “RL” indicates General and Specific Restrictions apply (e.g., RL4013099).  
 
“Section 2”: Specifies the date the Protection Notice was issued. Specifies the characteristics of the shipment,  including the car 
number(s), car marshaling, type of lading, shipper/origin, consignee/destination, full route, and CPKC routing.  
 
“Section 3”:  Specifies the measurements of the shipment:  height, width, length, gross weight, center of gravity from the truck 
center and the combined center of gravity.  
 
“Section 4”:   Specifies the subdivision name and the mileage points between which the protection  notice applies on the 
subdivision. Specifies the W-code Classification.  
 
“Section 5”:  Specifies the “Specific Restrictions” that apply to a load at precise locations along its routing.  They are listed by 
mileage in the sequence in which they will be encountered.  Some examples are  reduce speed over bridges or passing specific 
obstructions; stop, examine, and proceed with crew observing the movement; and special marshaling.  
 
“Section 6”:  Specifies the “Code 6 Instruction message” and file number of the Protection Notice.  The “Code 6 Instruction 
message” on the train consist must be exactly as shown in Section 6 of the Protection Notice.

When requesting permission from the Train Dispatcher or Operations Supervisor, the employee doing so must supply the following

• Car initials and number,  
• Classification (such as W-03, or W-03-07),  
• Specific Restrictions, if any,

the protection of such shipment. 
 
5.3 Protection of Moves  
Where Yardmasters or other employees in charge of movements are on duty to instruct moves, the Train Dispatcher or Operations 
Supervisor will notify them of the presence of dimensional shipment in a train before that train enters the yard under their 
jurisdiction.  The Yardmaster or other employee in charge of movements within these yards will be responsible to keep crews 
informed of the location of conflicting dimensional traffic within those yards, while on duty.  Train Dispatcher or Operation s 
Supervisor will provide for protection against main track movements as outlined in Item 5.3.

sections.text:
Section 6 – Dimensional Equipment 
 
 
66 
  
5.4 Operating Through Yards, Sidings, Interchange Track and Within Yard Limits    
Crews must be especially watchful when operating through yards, sidings, interchange tracks and yard limits to ensure ample side 
clearance exists between dimensional traffic being handled and equipment on adjacent tracks.  
 
Crews must also ensure ample side clearance exists between equipment being handled and dimensional traffic on adjacent tracks.  
 
Where overhead or side clearance is doubtful, movement must be stopped, and inspection made to ensure that adequate 
clearance exists before proceeding.  
 
5.5 Marshaling of Dimensional Shipments  
Unless otherwise indicated in the car marshaling instruction of the protection notice, dimensional shipments may be marshaled  
without restriction. However, to permit visual observation by the crews, the dimensional shipments requiring a physical examination 
in order to clear a specific location, shall be marshaled as close as possible to the lead locomotive.  
 
On trains operating without a manned caboose, all dimensional traffic that would normally be marshaled to permit visual 
observation by the crew shall be marshaled as close as possible to, but not more than 2000 feet from the controlling unit.    
 
Note: Train consist, or protection notice will indicate dimensional shipments to which this item applies. 
 
5.6 Movement Past Other Traffic Adjacent Track  
When the dimensions of traffic do not permit unrestricted movement past other traffic on adjacent tracks and it is not practicable 
for the Train Dispatcher or Operations Supervisor to maintain blocking devices or to withhold operating authority, the Train 
Dispatcher or Operations Supervisor may use verbal  
instructions or issue a track bulletin to protect restricted meets against other main track movements.  
 
5.7 Joint Trackage   
Prior to a dimensional shipment being moved over joint trackage, permission must be obtain from the concerned railroad(s).  
 
5.8 Switching   
Dimensional shipments are not to be humped or kicked.

US Southern Region CALL Program  
The US Southern Region  has developed a program for employees to report unsafe motorist behavior and 
trespassing on CPKC property. The program has been named the KCSR CALL Program.   
 
The program has two purposes:  
1. To establish a process that will allow employees to report unsafe motorists, unsafe pedestrians, and trespassers.  
2. To use the employee report information to follow up with local and state enforcement agencies.  
To use the KCSR Call program, employees should notify the KCSR train dispatcher or call the Critical Incident 
Desk (CID) at 877-527-9464 when any of the following circumstances occur:  
• Vehicle goes around a lowered gate  
• Vehicle crosses in front of a close approaching train  
• Vehicle stops or traffic “stacking” onto crossing  
• School bus does not STOP at a crossing.  
• Haz-Mat vehicle fails to STOP at crossing.  
• Pedestrians fouling railroad tracks or crossings  
• Individual is trespassing on KCSR property  
 
The KCSR would like to thank everyone in advance for participating in this team effort to improve rail safety.
